a.notes: Through the owner's eyes, the track series earns its second look. Its fine steel lines, lamps, buffers and timetable margins run on every page, and that is the language the owner called high style. This round Lit Sill Line (t2-track-graft) is the design that best answers 'the changes need to reflect more of the page content'. It rebuilds Home rather than recolouring it, and it brings back the original tube's light (lit run, airglow, the lamp wire, lamps on scanlined glass) exactly where the phosphor means now and live, while the family's words sit on grounded ink. Grafted features that WORKED: in Lit Sill Line, the greeting standing on the Coming up rail (Pocket's NOW-to-NEXT idea rebuilt as track), Status's annunciator moved onto the glass, the ink plates for the family's words, and the line carried onto the month. In Night Interchange, the interchanges naming where a message lands, and the service board's lit tiles. In Pocket Diary, the diary date stacks (a typesetting gain the owner will enjoy) and the weekend bands on the glass. In Pocket Restacked, the kind-capped cartridges, which add colour. Grafted features that did NOT work, or not yet: in Lit Sill Line, 'Coming up' is displaced under the sill and 'All plans' dangles below the plates. Night Interchange runs a second rail on General beside the settings rail. Pocket Diary puts the key in every footer, and its amber head tally is too loud. Restacked's full-width panorama leaves empty lit glass in the middle. Branch Lines, Condensed (the type-only mutant) changes too little to see. Refinements: Trued (t2-track-refine) is the most finished signal box, but moving the tube down cost the first screen its light. The next Trued should take Lit Sill Line's lit run from the greeting down to the rail, and the two would converge on a very strong design. Relaid, Finished and the two Pocket refinements are careful, but at a thumbnail they read as their parents, and the owner has said plainly that near-identical is not enough. Across the whole heat the remaining gap is the same: outside green and amber, colour is still mostly grey steel. The owner asked for grounded colour in solid things with a job (Lit Sill Line's ink plates are the one clear example). A measured period cool (the plans' cyan caps, a slate-blue plate for the family) would lift every lineage without adding glow.

scores.why: This is the heat's biggest change to the page itself. The greeting stands on the Coming up line: the NOW lamp, a lit run with airglow rising off it, and Next up dropping a lit wire onto the rail. Status draws its lamps on scanlined glass, so the original tube's light is back where it means something. The family's things sit on grounded midnight-ink plates that show even at a squint, and fine track art runs on every page, the month included. What holds it back: the 'Coming up' head is stranded under the sill on the left, after its own plates, and the plate names wrap.

The line art is exactly what the owner praised. The Next up tube hangs from tomorrow's stop like any other plate, the setup is a numbered track that ends at a buffer, and To do's NOW runs across the full row. Status becomes one instrument with labelled lamps and a tally, and 'What's the plan?' is the best title here. With the tube moved down, the top of Home is a box and three keys with less phosphor. Colour is still mostly slate and green, with only small rings of cyan and amber.

The best typesetting in the heat. Every date is set as a diary sets a day, with a big figure beside a small month and weekday, on Home, Plans and To do. These rows are close kin of the Galley Rack Coming up strips the owner admired. It keeps one steel spine from NOW to LATER and adds weekend bands on the glass. Colour is almost all steel, grey and amber, though, and the amber '6 worth a look' in Status's head is loud for six odd calls.

The ways to start become interchanges, each naming in its line's enamel where the message will land (Plans, To do, Ideas). That is line art that explains the product. Status is a service board of lit 'Working' tiles, a good use of phosphor on solid plates. At a thumbnail Home is still the parent's three columns, the title breaks onto two lines at desktop, and the colour beyond the enamel hairlines is thin.

Finely finished signal-box work on every page. The setup and Status rails run vertically, the chat hangs in a timetable margin, the form has its rail, and each count stands at its line's buffer. Its title, 'What shall we plan?', beats Revival's pun. But Home is nearly identical to its parent, which is the owner's 'those look nearly identical' complaint, and the grounded colour is thin.

Clean and calm: every list is posted along dotted leaders, To do is a one-line timetable with times in the margin, and 'What's our plan?' is set large. But it is about 90% green by share of colour, the enamel roundels are the only other hue, and Vera's line is drawn mostly on Home, so the line language thins out on the other pages.

Solid and orderly. The shelf gets its own line, Status rows hang lamps on the spine, and 'What's our plan?' is set well. At a thumbnail it reads as its parent, and the page is mostly grey slate with little grounded colour in solid things.
A strong base: a double-track chat, a line from home on Ideas and a To do timetable. Its Status lamps carry no labels, it is 90% green by share, and 'What's next for us?' narrows the job.
The purest Signal Box line language: vertical setup and Status rails, a chat in a timetable margin, a form rail. 'What shall we line up?' is a pun on the motif, and there is little grounded colour.

A real restack. The panorama tube spans the width, Coming up sits beside To do, and the kind-capped cartridges bring welcome colour to Lately added. But the wide tube has empty lit glass between the words and the trace, the first screen looks like the parent's, and it keeps 'next for us' (as the dice rule requires).
One spine through every page, a lit NOW/NEXT column and good date blocks. It is mostly grey and carries the parent's To do clutter ('Edit, complete, or snooze' on every row).
The Plex Condensed legends are tidy, but only the type changed and it is nearly invisible at page scale. It carries its parent's monochrome Chat and Status and the 'next' title.
The station idea reads well on Home and in Chat. Its To do rows are three lines deep, the palette is mostly green and grey, and it keeps 'What's next for us?'.
The scale under the departure board, drawing days to each plan, is line art that means time, and I would keep it. The drawn emblems on every head are costume, and most pages are unchanged.
The yardstick is well structured and grounded, with a real glow in its tubes. It has little of the track line art the owner loves, and it still lights 'mind' in 'What's on your mind?'.

The original glow is here, but so are the monochrome green, the contrast (ink contrast 17.1 on the measures table) and the Matrix look the owner asked to calm. It has no line art, and the title is 'What's on your mind?'.

fixes.suggestion: KEEP: the greeting standing on the Coming up rail; the NOW lamp and lit run with airglow; the tube's power lamp dropping a lit wire to the rail; Status's lamps and scanlines on the glass; the midnight-ink plates for what the family wrote (chat, Coming up plates, the month's plans); the line on the month; 'What are we planning?'. FIX: (1) Home: 'Coming up' sits under the sill at the left, after its own plates in reading order. Make it the rail's name plate at the terminus above the line (like a station board), with the Calendar note in small print beside it, and stand 'All plans' at the buffer, as setup's 'All the setup steps' already does. (2) The plan plates wrap to two-line names. Give each plate its share of the rail's width (let the four fill it) or balance the names to one line with the time below. (3) Give the plan plates the plans' cyan 2px cap on their ink, so a plan is told from a chat message at a glance, and keep the ink off boards, rows and text so the navy stays measured (the owner found Navy Room 'more blue than necessary'). (4) Status: put small labels under the lamps on the glass (Refine's 'Chat Digest Lookups…'), and pull the tally and 'Change the limit' together, beside or just under the glass, so the right half of the page isn't empty slate. (5) Month: fold the past weeks as Refine does, so the line opens on this week. (6) To do: carry Refine's full-width NOW line across the rows. (7) Phone: shorten the empty band beside the tube's foot.

KEEP: the tube hanging from tomorrow's stop; the numbered setup track ending at a buffer; the Status instrument with labelled lamps and its tally; the full-width NOW on To do; the folded month; 'What's the plan?'. FIX: (1) The top of Home lost its phosphor. Graft the Lit Sill Line's idea: a NOW lamp at the greeting board's foot whose lit run drops into the Coming up rail, with airglow, so the first screen has light again. (2) The four short plates leave slate under them beside the tall tube. Hang each plate's facts (kind ring, who) so they fill the tube's height, or put the tube at the right end. (3) Grounded colour in solid things: give the family's plates (chat, the month's plans) a solid ink or slate-blue fill, not just a 3px bar. (4) The '5 coming' count should come from the view, not the capped list.

KEEP: the chat in a timetable margin, counts at the buffers, the five-shape lamp legend, the vertical setup rail, 'What shall we plan?' (or 'What's the plan?' if 'shall' reads stiff). FIX: Home needs a visible change, or it reads as Revival. Take the tube-at-first-stop or the lit sill line so the phosphor belongs to the week. Make the plates hang to the right of their stops so the date comes first in reading order. Give the form rail a stop inside 'Everything else' so it has no long empty run, and pass the month's count from the view.

KEEP: the interchanges naming Plans / To do / Ideas in their enamel; the departure board's refresh; Status as a service board of lit tiles; the forms as lines to a terminus. FIX: (1) 'What are we planning?' breaks onto two lines in the centre column at 1280. Widen the centre column or set the title one step smaller so it holds one line. (2) Raise the interchange destination words from 13px to 14-15px and make the leader darker. (3) Break the parent's three-column silhouette: for example, run Vera's line full width at the top, with the board as its first departure. (4) Bring grounded colour into solid things, not only hairlines: a solid ink plate for the family's chat bubbles, and the enamel on the section-head tiles. (5) Drop the second rail on the General settings page.

KEEP: the diary date stacks (big figure, small month and weekday) on every dated row; the NOW/NEXT/LATER spine; the weekend bands on the glass; 'Anything to plan?' or 'What's our plan?'. FIX: (1) Colour: nearly everything that isn't green is grey steel. Give the family's things a grounded plate (slate-blue or ink) and show the Plans cyan on the month in each stack at full strength, so the page isn't green and grey alone. (2) Status: set '6 worth a look' in ink with a small amber lamp, since the demo's odd calls aren't a crisis. (3) Home LATER rows: bring 'for …' and '#n' in beside the title (a set measure, or a drive column) to close the wide gap. (4) To do: drop the separate time column where 'due tomorrow, 19:56' already says the time. (5) Put the footer key only on pages whose shapes need it (Status, Settings), so every footer isn't a legend.

KEEP: the posted leaders, the one-line To do timetable and the large 'What's our plan?'. FIX: carry Vera's line past Home (Status and Settings rows as stops) and give the enamels a job in solid things, since at about 90% green by share of colour it reads monochrome.

KEEP: Coming up beside To do, and the kind-capped cartridges in Lately added. FIX: shorten the panorama tube, or fill its middle with the four weeks' labels, so no lit glass stands empty, and change the title from 'next' (the rule allows it once it is no longer a dice mutant).

a.titles: Best: 'What are we planning?' (t2-track-graft, t2-timetable-graft) and 'What's the plan?' (t2-track-refine). 'What are we planning?' is the household's own present tense, it invites the family to tell Vera what is on the go, and its lit word is the job itself. On Lit Sill Line it stands directly above the lit line of plans that answers it, which is the title and the page speaking together. It holds one line on a phone, but in Night Interchange's narrow centre column it breaks onto two lines at desktop, which weakens it there. 'What's the plan?' is the shortest and most kitchen-table, and 'plan' covers weekends, ideas, the calendar, reminders and wishes. 'What's our plan?' (t2-timetable-refine, t2-pocket-refine) is as good, with the family's 'our'. 'Anything to plan?' (t2-pocket-graft) is warm and open, but it can read as a yes/no question ('Anything?' 'No'), so it is a lighter invitation. 'What shall we plan?' (t2-track-refine2) is a real improvement on Revival's pun and keeps the job lit, but 'shall' is a little formal for a family. Weaker: 'What's next for us?' (t1 carried designs and the three dice mutants). It narrows the job to what comes next, since ideas to keep and wish lists are not 'next', and it lights a second 'next' beside the NEXT UP tube. 'What shall we line up?' (t1-track-revival) lights the motif rather than the job. Fails: 'What's on your mind?' (both yardsticks), the owner's own complaint: it says nothing of planning.

scores.why: This is where the soul comes from: the greeting's pool, full halos, a real radar tube and breathing lamps. But the glow washes over every greeting border, pill and card edge, so it reads as glare rather than scarcity (the family's 'Matrix'), and the tubes decorate the page more than they carry it.

Every page has a tube that carries its own data (the gauge, the To do bars, the question typed on the glass), and the glow elsewhere is scarce. It is still a strong benchmark for meaningful light, but the page around the tubes is flat grey and the lit word is 'mind'.

The Ideas 'line from home' strip chart, the Status shelf of glowing lamps and the lit month run are real phosphor instruments drawn from the page's own data. Home is still its parent's greeting, though, and Chat and Status run about 90% green.

It has the best big lit title of round 1 over the original greeting pool, and a lamp legend that holds from Status to Settings. But its lit word 'line' is the motif, not the job, and Home is otherwise quiet. Its refinement now does the same job better.

The Next up tube now hangs from the first stop of the Coming up line, so the green screen is the main line's first lamp. Ideas' line from home names its stations in blooming VT323, Status is one bezel holding the spend tube and a labelled lamp board, and Chat ends at a lit 'your turn'. The phosphor sits where something is now, on calm slate. Only the top of Home is a little dimmer than before, and row afterglow is still hard to see.

'What shall we plan?' is set big and condensed with a true two-layer halo over the greeting pool, beside a proper bezelled tube. The setup line lights its 'Next step', and the focused field's stop glows on its own centre line. The light is well rationed, but Home keeps its parent's layout, so less of the page content changed.

The truest return of the original light in the heat, and all of it is content. The greeting stands on the Coming up rail. A lit run goes from 'now' to the tube, whose power lamp drops a glowing wire to the rail, and airglow rises off that run. On Status the spend tube carries the Who answers, Keys and Connected lamps on its own glass. Everything else is grounded: the family's plates in midnight ink, steel rails, bone figures.

The condensed Plex legends suit an engraved signal panel, and the light is the parent's. But it adds no new phosphor, Chat and Status stay nearly all green, and the dotted zeros reach into Vera's own words. That reads machine-like rather than lit.

The dot-matrix departure board is a convincing 1980s green screen listing real departures, beside a lit terminus and the newest chat stop aglow. The yellow counts in the bar and the loud amber still spend the scarcity.

The board prints the next plans on phosphor leaders and powers on with a raster fill. Vera's line ends in a glowing terminus, 'plan' carries the halo, and the afterglow is a visible green edge at 120ms. Everything else is matte slate with posted dotted leaders and grounded enamel roundels. Chat still leans almost all green, and at a squint the board outshines the box.

The board refreshing with a line of light as Home opens is the most tube-like behaviour in the heat. Status's lit 'Working' readout windows are glowing dots on the black, set in sunk wells. But the enamel interchange stubs push other-colour neon to 14.7%, and 'planning' breaks onto its own line in the narrow middle column.

The steel survey scales are drawn in hairlines outside the glass, so they add drawing, not light. The 72px emblems and dimension marks are drafting costume. Only the NOW lamp at each datum is new phosphor.

Time is drawn in light: lit NOW and NEXT plates, a square-pulse trace of the coming weeks, a lit NOW line through To do. But the chamfered cartridges are costume, and the afterglow is amber, a kind colour, not phosphor.

The cartridges are gone, the tube's tag says TOMORROW, and Status's lamps sit on the line as glowing nodes with 'On' and 'Off'. A lit NOW plate stands beside the spend tube, and pointing at a plan lights its pulse on the glass: light that answers. It is calm and correct, but Chat and the page heads are unchanged, so the phosphor story is mostly Home's and Status's.

The glass carries more of the page now: weekends shaded on the trace, and today's figure '30' lit beside NOW on Home and on the Plans agenda. Every dated row reads as a diary line of light numerals on slate, and a lamp key sits in every footer, which is a system. The loud amber '6 worth a look' at Status's head spends scarcity on demo noise, and the afterglow doesn't show.

The full-width NEXT panorama repeats the 5:1 tube shape that was faulted before, since period screens were near 4:3. The chamfered cards stay, and the eased weights make the lit words slightly less alive rather than calmer.

fixes.suggestion:
KEEP:
- the board's line-of-light refresh as Home opens (the best phosphor behaviour in the heat);
- Status as a service board of sunk readout windows with glowing lamps, and its legend;
- the interchanges that say where a message lands.
FIX:
(1) 'planning' breaks onto its own line on desktop. Widen the middle column to hold the title on one line, or use 'What's our plan?'.
(2) The enamel stubs, key caps and names on the interchanges push other-colour neon to 14.7%. Lower their chroma to grounded enamel (sky and teal near C 0.06) and make the line's name 14-15px, not 13px.
(3) Home is still three columns. Let Vera's line visibly run into the board (the board as the first departure), so the structure changes as well as the detail.

KEEP only the NOW lamp at the scale's datum. Draw the scale INSIDE the board's glass in phosphor (days to each departure as lit ticks), not as steel hairlines under it. Drop the 72px emblems and the dimension ticks on heads, which are costume.

Restacking Home by rows of the line is a good structural idea. Keep it, but make NEXT a near-4:3 tube beside a wide trace strip rather than one 5:1 panorama glass. Drop the chamfered cards, and keep the eased weights off the lit words so the halo keeps its core.

a.titles:
Best: 'What's our plan?' (t2-timetable-refine, t2-pocket-refine) and 'What are we planning?' as set in t2-track-graft.

'What's our plan?' is the household's own kitchen question, and 'our' carries the family's voice. Its lit word is the job, and a short noun like 'plan' takes E1's two-layer halo cleanly at 40-44px, so the one glow reads as light rather than colour.

'What are we planning?' is present tense and invites the family to tell Vera what is on the go. In Lit Sill Line the lit line of plans directly below answers it, so question and light are one idea, and the longer lit word carries more bloom. In t2-timetable-graft the same words break onto two lines in the narrow middle column, which weakens it there.

Close behind:
- 'What's the plan?' (t2-track-refine): the shortest and most job-true, but it echoes the placeholder.
- 'Anything to plan?' (t2-pocket-graft): the most open invitation, since anything can be told, but a touch casual.
- 'What shall we plan?' (t2-track-refine2): the best-set title typographically (40px condensed, halo, largest head), but 'shall' is stiff.

Weaker: 'What's next for us?' (the mutants and the carried grafts). It rhymes with NEXT UP, so its lit word competes with the tube's legend beside it, and an idea to keep or a wish list is not 'next'. 'What shall we line up?' (the carried revival) lights the motif, not the job.

a.notes:
Through this lens the heat is led by the designs that turn the page's own content into the light, not by the tidiest ones.

Grafts that worked:
- Track, Lit Sill Line: the airglow reworked as light rising off the lit run, since it has a source and a meaning. The 'ink' rule (the family's words on midnight plates) is the best grounded companion in the heat, because it has a job. The lamps typed on Status's glass, annunciator-style, and the month's line both carry the diagram onto pages that had none.
- Timetable, Night Interchange: the interchanges (from the switchboard idea of each cell naming its page, rebuilt as a station's interchange) are the heat's most useful invention; they teach what the box does. The board's refresh on opening brings back the tube's life. The service board in words is sound but over-plated.
- Pocket, Pocket Diary: the diary date setting is a lovely typographic graft that pays off on four pages, and the weekend bands on the glass are subtle and right.

Grafts that did not work:
- Pocket Diary's footer key: it reads as fine print.
- Night Interchange's second rail on the settings pages: one line too many.

Dice mutants:
- The Condensed mutant's Plex superfamily drifts toward IBM Carbon, a well-known house style, and loses DM Sans's warmth.
- The Surveyed mutant's emblems are costume, but its survey scale is a keeper.
- The Restacked mutant's panorama tube is the most cinematic phosphor on show and should be grafted into Pocket Diary.

Refinements:
- Relaid, Finished and Pocket Timeline, Trimmed are honest finishing work, but their Homes look nearly identical to their parents, which is the fault the owner named.
- Branch Lines, Trued's tube hung from the rail is its boldest idea, but it cost the greeting its glow.

Phosphor:
- Every design here has put the halo, the bloom and the scanlines back in the tubes. The ones that also light the NOW lamp and its run (Lit Sill Line, the track family, Night Interchange's lit terminus) come closest to the owner's 'light where attention belongs'.

Yardsticks:
- Desk Terminal, Joined (7) stays a fair bar.
- Lit Sill Line clears it, and Night Interchange and Pocket Diary edge past it on character.

scores.why: The most memorable Home in the heat. The greeting stands on its own Coming up rail, a lit wire drops from the tube's power lamp to the line, the now lamp breathes and airglow rises off the lit run. So the page's own content becomes the Phosphor light, which is exactly the owner's test. The midnight 'ink' plates for what the family wrote give a grounded second colour with a clear job, and the lamps typed on Status's glass carry the same language to another page.

The interchanges are a real invention: each way to start names the line it lands on, with an enamel stub. The departure board refreshes line by line as the page opens, and Status reads as a station's service board. Warm ink, steel and enamel around a phosphor board make a clear, grown-up station-at-night mood. It is marked down because the title breaks onto two lines in the narrow centre column, and the service board's wall of plates is heavy.

Pocket Diary finds a typographic identity of its own: a big numeral with the month and weekday stacked beside it, set the same way on Home, Plans, To do and Chat. It has a lit '30' at NOW, weekend bands on the glass, and LATER as the diary's notes pages across the foot. It is charming and could only be this app. The footer key is small print, and Home's outline still reads as its parent's at a glance.

This is the most finished typography in the heat. The heads are set in wide Archivo like station signage, with enamel roundels and a short enamel lead under each head, and every list is posted with dotted leaders. 'What's our plan?' sits on one line, large, above a departure board. It is a lovely, quiet poster of a page, but it carries fewer new ideas than its graft, and Chat is still almost all green.

Hanging the tube from the first stop on the rail is a bold structural idea: the monitor becomes part of the diagram. Status's labelled-lamp instrument and the NOW rule across To do are well finished. But the greeting has lost most of its phosphor, and the 'Or start with' column is plain outlined boxes that do not speak the track language.

The full-width panorama tube, with the words, the weeks traced as pulses and the radar across the whole width, is the single most cinematic piece of phosphor in the heat. The denim secondary keys are a tasteful quiet companion. The rest is the parent unchanged, and the first screen looks the same as before.

It keeps a strong line language on every page: the chat as a track down the middle, To do's time rail, Ideas' 'line from home' strip chart and the month's line. Home's greeting is still the original's, though, and the page is mostly slate and green.
A fine founding idea: Vera's line down the middle of Home and a dot-matrix departure board. It is let down by the numbered nav reading as counts and by yellow links beside amber late.
The NOW, NEXT and LATER spine, the oscilloscope tube with a pulse per plan, and the month as a green screen make a clear idea. The notched idea cards and boxy filters are the dated part of it.
It is calmer and more consistent: the written key, lamps as nodes on the line, the amber setup shelf and the TOMORROW tag. It is a sound tidy-up of its parent that adds no new character.

Status's inline tally and the plan caps are well finished, and the chat's feeder lines are handsome. But Home is nearly identical to the revival, which is exactly what the owner objected to, and 'What shall we plan?' reads stiff.
Its chat is lovely: times in the margin and bubbles hanging off horizontal feeders. The title's lit word 'line' is the motif, not the job, and Home is otherwise the parent's.

The steel survey scale under the board, dimensioned '5 plans in 24 days', is a charming idea worth keeping. The 72px drawn emblems and the tick marks on every head rule are costume that busies the heads.
Setting the lineage in IBM Plex Condensed moves it towards IBM's Carbon look rather than a signal box of its own. The dotted zero in Vera's prose is fussy, and at page size the change hardly shows.
A coherent system with a character of its own: numbered sections, a monitor leading each page, Status's VU meter and To do's bar screen. It is sometimes more engineered than lovely.
It has its own look, but that look is a green wash over stock dark cards: the 'Matrix' feel the family named, with little that grounds it.

fixes.suggestion: KEEP: the greeting standing on the Coming up rail; the tube's power-lamp wire dropping to the lit run; the breathing now lamp; the airglow off the run; ink plates for the family's words; Status lamps typed on the glass with the big tally; the month's line. FIX Home: (1) Set 'Coming up' ABOVE the rail's left end, like a board's name plate beside the now lamp, instead of stranded under it with the calendar note. (2) Put 'All plans' at the rail's T buffer as the buffer's label, as setup does, not 40px below the plates. (3) Plate names wrap to three lines ('Mount St. / Helens day trip'). Give the plates one more column of width or set names at 14px in the head face, so each is two lines at most. (4) The #182536 ink plates with pale caps sit close to a stock 'selected' navy. Warm the ink a touch (a blue-black nearer #1a2230, with a #86a9cc cap only), so it reads as ink on paper, not as a selection. (5) To do and Lately added below are the parent's. Carry the ink rule into them (the family's own words as ink rows), so the lower half also shows the new language. Status: pull the tally closer to the glass or give it a lamp column, since 160px of slate stands empty beside it. Plans: open the month on the week holding today, with past weeks folded to a strip. Phone: fill the empty glass beside the prompt in the tube's foot band.

KEEP: the tube hung from tomorrow's stop; Status's labelled-lamp instrument; the NOW rule across To do; the named setup stations. FIX: make 'Or start with' a short branch line off the box (three stops with a terminus), not three outlined buttons, so the greeting speaks the track language. Give the greeting back some phosphor: the lit word's two-layer halo, and the box's frame lit while focused. Stop Coming up's plate names breaking onto two lines at desktop width.

KEEP: the interchanges (enamel core, stub and the line's name at the key's end); the board's line-by-line refresh on opening; the month's departed weeks folded; Status stated in words. FIX: (1) The title wraps to 'What are we / planning?' in the centre column. Either set it at about 2.1rem, or use 'What's our plan?' in the refine's wide Archivo, so it holds one line. (2) Raise the key-to words to 14px and give their leader more contrast; they are the idea, so they must be readable. (3) Status: keep plates only for Working and Needs a look. Show 'Not set up' as a ring and words with no plate, so the service board is not a wall of identical boxes. (4) Take the refine's wide Archivo heads, enamel leads and dotted leaders across every list, and one system is finished. (5) Chat: give Vera's bubbles warm ink rather than green, so Chat is not 96% green.

KEEP: the wide Archivo heads, enamel roundels and 3rem leads, the dotted leaders on every list, the time-first departure board, and steel-denim links. FIX: graft in the interchanges from Night Interchange (the starters naming their line). Give Chat colour beyond green (warm ink for Vera's bubbles, a bone initial disc). Show the board's power-on refresh as prominently as the graft does.

KEEP: the diary date setting (big numeral with month and weekday stacked) on every dated row, the lit '30' at NOW, the weekend bands on the glass, LATER as full-width notes, and 'Anything to plan?' in the condensed head. FIX: (1) Drop the footer key or move it to the page head at 13px; as it stands it is legal print nobody will read. (2) Status's amber '6 worth a look' shouts about harmless calls; show it in pewter unless something is really wrong. (3) The LATER rows leave a wide gap between the title and 'for …'. Set a measure, with 'for' at about 60% of the row and #n in the margin. (4) Take the mutant's full-width panorama tube for NEXT on desktop, so the first screen changes as much as the typography does. (5) Ideas' filters are still a boxed panel; hang them from the spine like To do's quick add.

KEEP: the full-width NEXT panorama (words, the weeks traced as pulses, the radar) and the denim secondary keys. FIX: on the phone, move setup after the tube so NEXT is on the first screen. Replace the notched idea cards with the diary rows.

a.titles:
Best: 'What's our plan?' (t2-timetable-refine, t2-pocket-refine) and 'What shall we plan?' (t2-track-refine2).
- 'What's our plan?' is 16 characters and holds one line anywhere. 'Our' makes it the household's question, and the lit word is the job itself.
- Typographically, the lit word closes the line against the question mark, so the eye lands on it last.
- The finest setting of any title in the tour is timetable-refine's Archivo expanded 600 at 40px.
- 'What shall we plan?' carries Relaid's 'we' at 40px condensed 700 and reads warm, not stiff, in that bold setting.

Also good: 'What's the plan?' (t2-track-refine). It is the shortest and most kitchen-table of the titles, but a little less personal than 'our'.

Mixed:
- 'What are we planning?' (t2-track-graft, t2-timetable-graft) is warm present tense. But at 21 characters it is the longest. It breaks onto two lines in timetable-graft's desktop column, leaving 'planning?' alone, and eight lit letters make a heavier glow than one short word. The -ing form also reads more as a status check than an invitation.
- 'Anything to plan?' (t2-pocket-graft) invites anything, which fits the job, but it is a yes/no question to which 'no' is a complete answer.

Weak:
- 'What's next for us?' (the carried designs and the mutants) is warm, but 'next' narrows the job to the schedule and echoes the NEXT UP tube.
- 'What shall we line up?' (t1-track-revival) lights half a phrasal verb and names the motif, not the job.

Standard to adopt: 'What's our plan?', with 'What shall we plan?' as the track series' variant.

a.notes:
Walked through each design's own pages. The Wishes page and the Plans list view were not shot, so 'open a kid's wish list' was judged by the Home links (Maya and Theo are links on every design; Lit Sill Line folds wishes into one line at To do's foot, where they are easy to miss). No design has targets under 44px except Revival's one per page. The minimum text is 12-13px everywhere, and the minimum contrast is 5.15-5.26, so legibility at night is fine throughout. The usability differences are in structure and wording.

GRAFTS THAT WORKED: Night Interchange's ways to start that name their destination, and its Status as a service board in words. These are the two clearest 'what state is it in / what happens if I tap' improvements in the heat. Pocket Diary's diary rows and relative day words on Plans are the best answer to 'what's on this weekend'. Pocket Diary's footer key teaches the marks, though a design that needs a key on every page has too many marks. Trued's named Status lamps, its 'Or start with' column and its required-field markers on the form. Relaid's table-first Ideas with the radar beside it.

GRAFTS THAT DID NOT WORK: Lit Sill Line's Status lamps typed on the glass without names (a lookup puzzle). Its hover-only 'point at an idea to light its stop' (nothing for touch or keyboard). Pocket Diary's '6 worth a look' in amber at Status's head (an alarm for routine calls). Night Interchange's second rail on General (one rail too many).

MUTANTS: Condensed changes little for use; tabular figures in prose are the only cost. Restacked's pairing of Coming up with To do is sensible, but it keeps every parent fault. Surveyed's scales are too fine to read.

ACROSS THE HEAT: every Plans month and list disagree about the count ('1 plan in September', '2 coming by Sun 4 Oct', '5 coming'). One figure from the view, used everywhere, would fix that for all three lineages. The track series' phone Send is an arrow only, while the timetable and pocket designs keep the word 'Send'. Only the pocket refine and graft label Memory, Family, Status and Settings in the phone bar; everywhere else the heart icon alone must mean Memory. The timetable designs alone give desktop a Home link in the bar; a first-timer does not know the logo goes home. Relaid Finished and Revival lose the focus ring on an open select.

YARDSTICKS: every candidate except the carried t1-timetable-graft, t2-timetable-mut and the pocket mutant now matches or beats Desk Terminal for everyday use. Pocket Diary, Relaid Finished, Night Interchange and Pocket Trimmed beat it outright.

scores.why: 43 of 56 Home targets are under 44px. To do is a grid of cards with ISO dates ('Due 2026-09-27 19:56') and no late flag, so nobody can see at a glance what is overdue. 'What's on your mind?' does not say what the box is for.

Strong for tasks: the To do tube tallies late, this week, later and no date; the kinds are one-tap filters; Status has a numbered contents list. But the question and the box sit inside the tube as a terminal prompt, the title fails the job test, and the side panels push every list to the right.

Home reads cleanly: the box, the setup line, the Coming up rail and To do with a Due margin. Status has unlabelled lamp rows ('6 working · 7 off'), so nobody can tell which lamp is Gemini. The Plans head says '1 plan in September' while five are coming.

Its Status (a lamp legend and three panels) and its table-first Ideas are good. But the tracked capitals (DUE, WHO, MON), the pencil-only Edit on To do (a small target on every page), the open select with no focus ring and the pun title all cost a first-time user.

The best Home in its lineage for starting: 'Or start with' is a labelled column of keys. Setup says 'Next step'. Lately added shows what is already on the calendar. Status names every lamp, and the New idea form marks the required fields. Costs: the month opens folded to one week, so finding an earlier date takes a click; the Ideas strip's labels collide; the chat's Send falls below the 900px fold.

The calmest track design to use. The box has the tube beside it and the ways to start under it. Setup is a vertical list with 'Next step'. Ideas shows the table first, with the radar beside it. Status is one tally line with counts. The month is a full grid, To do shows date, #, who, relative due and Edit in words, and the chat composer is fully visible. Faults: the open select has no focus ring, Status says 'live' where every other page says 'working', and the month and the list give two different counts.

Home is compact: the whole diagram and every list fit in about 1.7 screens, and on the phone the lit line reaches the tube. But the 'Coming up' head sits under its rail, 'All plans' sits 40px from the buffer, the Status lamps on the glass have no names, the zero rows ('0 partly working · 0 stopped') add noise, 'point at an idea to light its stop' works only with a mouse, and the month head's '2 coming' disagrees with '5 coming'.

It is Branch Lines re-set in Plex, so it keeps the parent's task flow and the parent's faults (unnamed Status lamps, a Plans head reading '1 plan in September'). The condensed labels read fine, but tabular figures in prose ('$1.26', '10:00') are gappy, and the login head wraps to 'Sign in / to FamilyDB'.

A one-screen Home with 'Continue with Vera' is a real help. But the numbered bar ('1 Vera 2 Ideas 3 Plans') reads as counts of unread items, To do rows are three lines with an 'Edit, complete, or snooze' disclosure, and the labels are tracked capitals.

It fixes the parent's faults. The bar has Home and plain names, To do rows are one line with Edit, and the Status and Plans heads are sentences ('6 working · about $0.00 of $2.00 spent today'). Home shows everything on one screen. Costs: the box column is narrow for typing, and To do sits left of the box while coming after it in Tab order. To do's date stack is small, Ideas puts Kind before the idea's name, and month chips truncate ('Oaks Park roll…').

The ways to start say where the message will land (Plans, To do, Ideas), which answers a first-timer's 'what happens if I tap this'. Status is a service board that states each part's condition in words ('Working', 'Not set up', 'Needs a look'), and its head reads '5 working · 1 needs a look'. The month ends with 'October continues → Later'. Costs: 'What are we planning?' wraps to two lines in the narrow desktop column, the destination words are 13px, and General draws two rails.

It keeps the parent's counted-looking bar and three-line To do rows, and adds hairline scales with 12-14px figures under the screens. They read as texture rather than information, and the larger emblems make every head busier without helping any task.

The NOW/NEXT/Coming up spine is easy to follow. But on the phone Memory, Family and Status are folded under Settings, To do has two ways to add and 'Edit, complete, or snooze' on every row, and Ideas as notched cards is slower to scan than a table.

Clear and quick. The Home spine runs NOW, NEXT, Coming up, LATER beside a shelf of setup, To do, wishes and ideas. To do has one quick-add field with 'More: who, when, a reminder' and a Someday group. Plans is an agenda with a month tube, Ideas is a table, Status rows say On or Off in words, Settings lists what needs a look first, and the phone bar is labelled. Weaker points: the month grid is a picture on the tube, not a way to pick a date, and the amber half-lamp is never explained on Status.

The best at 'what is on, and when'. Every dated row (Home, the Plans agenda, To do, the chat) reads as big figure, month and weekday, time, entry, how far off, and the agenda says 'yesterday / today / tomorrow / in 4 days'. To do has a quick add, late rows sit above a lit NOW line, the key is in the footer, Settings leads with what needs a look, and the phone bar is labelled. Costs: '6 worth a look' in amber on Status sounds an alarm for routine calls, and on the phone To do's separate time column makes titles wrap.

Putting Coming up beside To do pairs the two dated lists sensibly. But the parent's usability faults stay: two ways to add on To do, long 'Edit, complete, or snooze' buttons, Ideas as cards, and Memory, Family and Status hidden under Settings on the phone. The denim secondary keys are too faint to guide anyone.

a.titles: BEST: 'What's our plan?' (t2-timetable-refine, t2-pocket-refine) and 'What's the plan?' (t2-track-refine). As the box's label they tell a first-timer exactly what the box is for, in the family's kitchen-table words. The lit word is the job itself, and they hold one line at every size shot, desktop and phone. 'our' makes it the household's question, so 'What's our plan?' edges ahead. CLOSE: 'Anything to plan?' (t2-pocket-graft) is the most open invitation: it reads as 'tell her anything that needs planning', so a reminder or an idea to keep fits. Its one risk is that it can be answered 'no'. GOOD BUT COSTLY: 'What are we planning?' (t2-track-graft, t2-timetable-graft) is warm present tense, but at 21 characters it wraps to two lines in Night Interchange's narrow desktop column, and the long lit word spreads the glow. 'What shall we plan?' (t2-track-refine2) is clear and lights the job, but 'shall' is a little formal for a family; 'What's our plan?' says the same thing more naturally. WEAKER: 'What's next for us?' (t2-track-mut, t2-timetable-mut, t2-pocket-mut, and the carried t1-track-graft, t1-timetable-graft and t1-pocket-graft) narrows the job to the schedule, and beside a NEXT UP screen it reads as a question the page has just answered. FAILS: 'What shall we line up?' (t1-track-revival) lights the design's own motif, not the job. 'What's on your mind?' (both yardsticks) could head any app. Recommendation for the standard: 'What's our plan?', with 'Anything to plan?' as the alternative.

a.notes: Near-duplicates: t2-track-mut is Branch Lines with only its type re-set, t2-track-refine2 is Signal Box Relaid with a new title, and t2-timetable-mut is Night Departures with drafting decoration. By the owner's test ('those look nearly identical'), none of the three earns its slot, and the carried t1 designs are now superseded by their t2 refinements. Grafted features that worked: Status lamps typed on the phosphor glass (track-graft), the lit run from the now lamp to the tube (track-graft), the greeting board whose foot is the Coming up rail (track-graft), the diary figure stacks and weekend shading (pocket-graft), head summaries under the page titles (timetable-refine and timetable-graft), the tube as the first stop on the Coming up line (track-refine), and cyan on-calendar rings in Lately added (track-refine). Features that did not work: the footer shape key (pocket-graft); the amber '6 worth a look' false alarm (pocket-graft); dark 'Not set up' slabs on Status (timetable-graft); navy ink plates in Chat on a double rail (track-graft); starter keys styled like fields (track-refine); folding the month to one week (track-refine); drafting ticks and emblems (timetable-mut); and condensed Plex (track-mut), which is invisible. Phosphor recovery: the best returns put light on live things built from data: the line from home on Ideas, Status lamps on glass, the pulses on the NEXT tube, the departure board, and the lit run on Home. No design in this heat goes back to glare. The pocket and track-graft/refine designs bring green down to 49-63% of the page's colour while keeping the spark. Timetable-refine, t1-track-graft and track-mut still sit at about 90% green, which is the Matrix risk that remains.

scores.why: This is the glare the owner complained about: green on green everywhere and 43 of 56 home targets under 44px. The phosphor sits everywhere, not only where attention belongs. It reads as the Matrix, not as a lit instrument.

A coherent, grounded system with the tube and the question lit at top-left, but it keeps the title the owner rejected. The numbered circles 1-5 on every section and the tracked-caps legends make Home read like a form, and Status is dense.

This is the one design where the phosphor and the structure are the same thing. a.titles: Best: 'What's the plan?' (t2-track-refine). It is short, sounds like the kitchen table, fits one line everywhere, and lights the job word, 'plan', which covers weekends, ideas, reminders and the calendar. A close second is 'What's our plan?' (t2-timetable-refine, t2-pocket-refine): it adds the household but reads a shade more like 'do we even have one?'. 'What are we planning?' (t2-track-graft, t2-timetable-graft) says the job in the present tense and works in Lit Sill Line's wide box. It fails in Night Interchange's narrow column, where it wraps to two lines at desktop width, and an eight-letter glowing word is a lot of halo. 'What shall we plan?' (t2-track-refine2) is stiff. 'Anything to plan?' (t2-pocket-graft) is a yes/no question and invites 'no'. It also sounds like a shop counter. 'What shall we line up?' (t1-track-revival) fails because it lights the motif, not the job, and 'line up' reads as queueing. 'What's next for us?' (t1-track-graft, t2-track-mut, t1-timetable-graft, t2-timetable-mut, t1-pocket-graft, t2-pocket-mut) fails: 'next' echoes the NEXT UP tube beside or below it, and it speaks of time alone, not of ideas, reminders or wishes.

b.notes:
In this heat, Flight Console's refinement and Figure Ground's refinement are the two designs that answer the owner's latest word. They change the content of each page (instruments that mean something, and rails that touch their rows) rather than tinting the old page. Both carry fine line art across pages, the owner's strongest positive signal, and both keep bright green for jobs, with slate, bone, steel and amber elsewhere.

console-refine edges ahead because it brings back more of the original tube's light: the meter tube with scanlines, jewels that glow, the green VT323 date window, the amber Late window's afterglow and the power-on radar. It does so without glare, and its steel-cyan flight plan is the period cyan the owner suggested in place of violet. figure-refine is the calmer and more typographic of the two, and its To do and Coming up rails are nearly the Signal Box lines the owner asked to see again. It needs more tube light, which its own mutant already shows how to add.

The Switchboard lineage has the most CRT greeting, 'plan' hot on the glass. But it stays 64-72% green, and its only lines are leaders, so through this lens it trails.

The grafts:
- Worked: console-graft's master caution band, lit bus and legs drawn over the month's weeks; figure-graft's round gauge tubes and folded empty weeks; switchboard-graft's radar numerals tied to the Plans rows (the best single graft in the heat).
- Did not work: console-graft's violet flight plan (off-period); figure-graft's pencil hatching and dimension lines (fussy and muddy); figure-graft dropping the chat's sequence diagram (it lost the lineage's best figure); switchboard-graft's circuit colours (too thin by area to offset the green tubes).

The mutants:
- Type (console-mut): small caps still read as tracked capitals, and nothing changes at page scale.
- Graphics (switchboard-mut): it gave Status real instruments but left Home alone.
- Phosphor (figure-mut): the right direction, but applied to the older layout.

Across the heat, the monitors' pewter cases are still thick and rounded (a standing owner complaint). The console lineage's 'here' key should be the dark latched key with a steel cap, not a pale steel slab.

scores.why: It has the tube's DNA: halos, a wash and a glowing radar. But it is almost all green on black, with ISO dates and boxy cards, and it keeps 'What's on your mind?'. It is the thing the owner asked to calm.

Grounded slate. Home has a Coming up track with NOW, To do has a NOW line, and the chat thread ends in a green ring. The tubes glow properly. But the title is still 'What's on your mind?', and much of Home is still boxes on boxes.

A real system: a figure on slate beside every section, bone ink, amber only for late, and the To do page's rail with a lit NOW line across the list. But Home's Fig. 1 is an abstract grid that stands apart from the rows it describes, and the tubes are dimmer than the owner now wants.

This is the line language the owner called high style, carried to every list. Home's Coming up, To do, the Plans month and the To do page each get a rail with lamps at the stops, dates in a timetable margin and leaders into the rows, and a glowing NOW line crosses each list. The chat is a sequence diagram. Grounded bone, blueprint and amber, with 'plan' lit. The faults: the blueprint sheets read navy at a squint, and the chat's 950px leaders.

The round 'Next in 1 day' tube on Plans and the folded empty weeks both work, and the Status gauge brings back real phosphor light. But the pencil-hatched kind squares are muddy, the dimension lines add noise to Coming up, and the chat has lost its sequence diagram for plain numbered arrows.

It brings the tube back where the manual shows phosphor. Plans gets a countdown screen, Status a lit spend tube, To do a lit next-due cell and the chat a lit newest arrow, which is what the owner last asked for. But Home keeps t1's detached figure and layout, so at page scale it reads close to its parent.

The instruments are strong: the flight plan, the moving-coil meter tube, the crew board of lamps and a wide radar on Ideas. But the zero-padded readout strip and the unlabelled T-minus ladders are codes the family has to learn. The chat's track stops at its head, and 'next' undersells the job.

The most complete answer to the owner. Bright green is lit only on instruments with jobs: the jewels, the live leg, the meter, the VT323 date window and the tubes. The Late 2 afterglows amber in a sunk window. Everything else is slate, steel, steel-cyan and matte clay and straw. The line art is on every page: the flight plan's legs labelled in days, the setup rail, and the chat hung from Vera's mark down to a green ring at the box, just as the owner praised in Signal Box. It changes what each page is, not its tint.

The master caution band, the lit bus joining the working lamps on Status, and the flight plan drawn over the month's weeks are all good ideas. So is the roll of light that runs down each tube as it switches on. But the flight plan is violet, which the owner called off-period, and Plans ends short with a large empty ground under one week.
Only the type changed, and at page scale it is the parent's page. The small-caps legends still read as tracked capitals, the slashed zeros make the zero-padding louder, and 'next' remains.

'What's the plan?' typed on the glass under a cursor is the most CRT-true greeting in the heat. The sommaire cells with page numbers and lamps are a real idea. But the page is 64% green, periwinkle leans violet, the lines are only dotted leaders with no tracks, and it is dense.

A lovely hot 'plan' on the glass. The two tiers are clear, and every inner page opens on a summary tube, which is a consistent system. But at 72% green it is the most monochrome candidate, the wide head tubes put green bands across every page, Home has empty ground at its foot, and there is no line art beyond leaders.

That is the best new idea in the lineage, and the big sky-blue day numerals are good typesetting. The setup line and contents foot keep Home compact. It is still 71% green, and 'Anything to plan?' invites a no.

The Status page gains real instruments: a moving-coil meter on the glass, rings of lamps round each cell's icon, and matte bone bars for what is past. The redrawn smiling monitor mark is charming. But Home is almost unchanged and the square-root scale is unexplained.

b.titles: The best is "Tell Vera what to plan." (Figure Ground). It names who hears you and the whole job in one verb, reads as an invitation to tell her something, and lights 'plan' at the line's end where the eye stops. It fits one line on a phone. A close second is "What's the plan?" (console-refine, switchboard-refine and switchboard-mut). It is the family's own kitchen-table phrase, the shortest, and lovely typed on the switchboard's glass. It does not say that Vera is the one listening, but the box and her mark beside it do. "What are we planning?" (console-graft) is good: the family's 'we', and 'planning' covers the ongoing job, but it is a little longer and softer. The two that fail are "Anything to plan?" (switchboard-graft), a yes/no question that invites 'no' and reads as a prompt rather than the planner's job, and "Tell Vera what's next." (t1-console-graft and its mutant). 'Next' leaves out ideas kept for someday and the wish lists, and it competes with the Next up tube beside it. Every candidate has dropped 'What's on your mind?', and only the yardsticks still carry it.

b.notes:
**Which grafted features worked**

- **Worked:**
  - the console graft's roll-bar power-on, a genuine tube behaviour, visible in its details strip
  - the master caution, one warm lamp with one job
  - the lit bus on Status, light that runs along a wire and means 'these answer'
  - the switchboard graft's radar moved onto the question's glass, with blips numbered by day and the lit '1' pair to the Plans list; the best tie between a tube and the page content in this heat
  - the switchboard graft's setup as one service line
  - the figure graft's round tube on Plans and its folded empty weeks
  - the pencil-hatched kinds, which are grounded and matte
- **Did not work, or needs a fix:**
  - the figure graft's dimension ticks, which read as ruler noise
  - Status dropping its live 'spent today' figure for a 30-day total
  - the switchboard graft's circuit-coloured leaders, which are too faint to count on a dim display
  - wide head tubes on every switchboard page: they are true to videotex but push bright-green pixels above today's page

**The three lineages through the Phosphor soul lens**

All three reflect page content rather than a colour wash, so each passes the owner's main test. They differ in how they bring the light back.

- **Console:** light as lamps, jewels and small windows. It is calm, and every light is live.
- **Figure Ground:** light as structure (the NOW trace) and as small tubes in drawings. The mutant shows the tube effects can return without breaking the manual.
- **Switchboard:** light as the screens themselves. It is the most vivid and the closest to the original's soul, but at risk of glare.

**Direction for next round**

The strongest direction for next round combines:
- the console graft's scarcity and behaviours (roll bar, lamps, bus)
- the switchboard graft's greeting glass with its numbered radar
- the figure mutant's rule that each figure's one live mark is lit

**Yardsticks**

Desk Terminal (8) still sets the bar for keeping one tube per page. Today's page (6.5) has the soul but not the scarcity.

scores.why: This design brings back the most of the tube's own behaviour and puts it only where something is live. A bar of light rolls down each tube as it switches on (a real CRT effect, clear in the details strip). Other light: the radar monitor, the meter tube on Status, a lit bus joining the models that answer, 'Working' lit in small windows, the live leg and Next jewel on the flight plan, and one warm amber caution lamp. Around it the slate and violet stay matte, so the page is calm without going dead.

The best green screen in the heat. The question, radar and cursor share one piece of curved glass ('Anything to plan? █'), and the blips carry day numbers, so the lit '1' on the glass matches the lit '1' leading the Plans list. That ties the light to the page's content. It loses points for area: every inner page opens on a wide, bright head tube, and bright-green pixels (6.66‰) are higher than today's (4.8‰), so it drifts back toward glare.

It answers 'bring some of that back' directly without losing the manual. The monitors bloom again behind scanlines in VT323 at three strengths. Plans gains a countdown screen. It also sets a rule the whole app could follow: each drawing's one live mark is a small lit tube (next due, the model in use, the newest arrow). Home still looks like its parent, and the smallest tubes ('#2', '04') are below the size where they read as screens.

The greeting sits in a lit pool with E7's scanlines. The readout rail has a lit Today tube and an amber window glowing behind 'Late 2'. Setup's next step is an amber jewel, and on Status 'Working' is lit in glass windows beside a real meter tube. Every light has a job and the page stays calm. Plans and To do rely on lamps rather than a screen, so those two pages are dimmer in spirit.

The spend meter is the best instrument in the heat: a moving-coil needle on real glass, with the average as a dashed ghost. Live things glow (rings of lamps round each Status cell) and past things are printed matte, which is exactly phosphor's logic. The mark becomes a miniature monitor with a power light. But Home is the parent's, and the bar's multicoloured place icons scatter colour without light.

'What’s the plan?' is typed alone on the glass, with 'the' dim and 'plan' white-hot, and Next up gets its own tube in the Plans cell. Every page opens on a green summary screen. It is the most alive, but also the greenest (72.5% share, 6.67‰ bright, above today), with two big tubes on Home, so the calm the tournament gained is partly spent.

This is a genuine terminal. Next up, the radar and 'What’s the plan?' share one glass, and there are tubes on To do, Plans and Status. The glow is contained in the screens, but the Home terminal is crowded, and the page reads nearly as green as the original in places.

It uses phosphor as structure: one lit NOW trace leaves each rail and crosses the list, and the next stop glows. It is lovely, and it means something on every list in time. The monitors are unchanged, and at a squint the blueprint grid sheets read as navy panels that compete with the green.

A convincing lamp panel: the radar monitor, the meter tube, the live leg, jewels and lit ladders. It is lively, but the zero-padded rail and the lit ladder bars spread small bits of light across rows where nothing is live.

The round tube on Plans ('Next in 1 day' on round glass inside an instrument ring) is a real new CRT instrument. The pencil-hatched kinds are nicely matte. But the round glass is dim, the tube sits on a grid sheet inside a frame so it is framed twice, and the dimension ticks add drafting noise without light. Status also traded the live 'spent today' for a 30-day total.

Its light is the parent's. Azeret figures and small-caps legends feel engraved, but the wider mono makes the zero-padded readouts louder and adds a fourth family, which takes a little from the tube voice.

A calm manual with the monitor, the lit 'plan', the lit wiring port on Status and a NOW line on To do. The phosphor is right but thin: Plans has no screen, and the blueprint sheets carry more visual weight than the light.

Yardstick. It is coherent and alive: the question under Next up on one glass, a tube on every page's left column (the To do bars, the Plans sparkline, the meter), and a breathing Ready lamp. Light is scarce and the tubes are real.

Yardstick. This is the soul itself: halos, bloom, scanlines and radar, all at full strength. But green sits on every border, pill and button across the page, so the light isn't scarce. It is the Matrix-like glare the owner called too bright.

The sight line runs title, box, Send, and To do's due queue with NOW is clear. Home's Fig. 1 is an abstract grid that does not line up with the Coming up rows, so you read the list twice. The lit tube on the left pulls the eye before the title.

Best reading of time in the heat. Each date sits level with its row, and one lit NOW line crosses To do between the late rows and the rest, and crosses Coming up above the next plan: you get it at a glance. The title comes first with the tube on the right, and the phone gets '4 more plans / 4 to do / 2 late' jump keys. Two misses: on Status, 'This page' shows a green lamp though it needs a look, and the chat's leaders draw long faint rules across the thread.

The folded month and the 'Next in 1 day' gauge make Plans quick to read, and the chat's numbered margin arrows are cleaner than the refinement's leaders. On Home the tube leads again, and Coming up leaves out tomorrow's hike, so NOW sits above a gap. The 'in 4 days' dimension marks are not to scale, and the hatched kind squares make seven kinds look alike.

Plans gains a real reading: its screen says 'Next in 1 day… then 1 more this week'. Home is the parent's, still with the abstract Fig. 1 and the tube first, and the new small tubes (#2, 04) are too small to read as states.

The Status lamps and meter read well. But six zero-padded readout links (05, 04, 02) come before the box in Tab order and sit above the greeting. The T-minus ladders have no labels, the crew board's dots are a code, 'next' narrows the title, and Send is only an icon on the phone.

The greeting now comes first, and the readout rail follows it in plain numbers. Every Status lamp carries its word (Working, Off, Needs a look), each leg of the flight plan shows its length, and setup marks its Next step. Faults: #4/#1 codes over dots on the To do crew board, a 60px gap between the box and the ways to start, ~800px dotted leaders on the Coming up rows, and Search fourth in Tab order on Ideas.

The master caution band is the clearest 'what needs you' in the tour: one line with its action, the same on Home, Status and Settings. The Plans month folds the weeks already gone and draws the legs over the week they belong to. Home fits one tall screen, and 'This page' finally reads amber. Against it: the tube leads the desktop greeting, Send is icon-only on the phone, and on Settings the caution's next step is bold words, not a link.

Type only. The small caps shrink the labels to about 8.7px glyphs ('BOOK THIS FAR AHEAD (DAYS)' reads slowly), Azeret makes the zero-padding louder, and the parent's faults stay: the rail before the box in Tab order, unlabelled ladders, 'next'.

The inner pages are the fastest to use, with the list at the top and the filters in a side rack. On Home, Next up comes before the title on the glass, and Vera, Silver Falls hike and '4 more' come before the textarea in Tab order. The page numbers (100 to 999) are a code the family must learn to ignore.

The eye goes title on the glass, the field inside it, then Send, and To do sits right under it. Every inner page opens on its list, and Settings puts 'needs a look' first, so things are found quickly. Weaknesses: the page numbers are still noise, the register leaders are almost invisible, the tags are lowercase, and the way-to-start links are announced with a leading '→'.

Plans rows led by big day numerals (1, 4, 9, 17, 24) scan faster than any date column here, setup is one line with its Next step, and the household pages make a compact foot strip. But the question shares the glass with the radar and gets a ~330px, two-line field. On the phone, the date and 'Each mark is a plan' push the question down, and the power-on briefly blanks the title and the field.

The spend meter's square-root scale reads as a wrong linear one, the ring segments are not numbered to their rows, and the Status heads lose their count leader. Home keeps the parent's Tab order and the tube before the title.
